old: Remember, meditation was a *Christian* thing long before it became the secularized, vaguely Buddhist, Californian thing most of us know it as today.[37] In fact, Dr. Jamie Kreiner, a professor of medieval history at UCLA, in her book *The Wandering Mind*, offered this gentle critique of the popular meditation origin story: "Ironically, the popular adoption (and appropriation) of South and East Asian practices in Europe and North America may have obscured our debts to the [Christian] monastic culture that seeded those concerns in the first place."[38]

old: In her book, which is about what we can all learn from ancient monks about staving off distraction, Dr. Kreiner points out that the early Buddhist monks' teaching on calming the mind with meditation comes from Turfan, a settlement along the Silk Road in China, where it just so happens that Christian missionaries flourished in the ninth and tenth centuries. That's not to say we shouldn't be wary of the spiritual syncretism and religious pastiche that's currently in vogue; it's to say meditation is just as much Sermon on the Mount as it is Siddhartha. The practice has ancient roots in Hebrew—and, later, Christian—spirituality. The difference is what we meditate *on*. As far back as Psalm 1, the people of God are invited to meditate "on his law day and night."[39] To fill our minds with Scripture, with truth.

old: Meditation on Scripture is a tried-and-true path for overcoming chatter—to quiet the roar of our brains and tune in to the gentle whisper of God. When I go into solitude, I'll often spend long stretches of time with my Bible open in my lap. I'll sit quietly in a short text, immersing my mind and heart in its truth. I find this approach to be especially helpful when my life is overtaxed and mind is jumpy or anxious; it's like a gentle pastor to my thoughts, nudging me away from chaos and into peace.
